newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy struggles to join EMU in 1999.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy struggles to join EMU in 1999.

text.p: Italy, fighting to control its finances and convince its EU partners that it is stable enough to help found a single currency, said on Wednesday it would launch a mini-budget to ensure that it was ready in time.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi met Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm a few hours after the government announced it had made up its mind to go ahead with a mini-budget, and said any delay to EMU's planned start in 1999 would be damaging.

Italy and the Netherlands, which currently holds the presidency of the European Union, said in a joint statement that the criteria and timetable for economic and monetary union laid down by the Maastricht Treaty had to be adhered to.
"Any delay...would jeopardise the credibility of the process towards EMU," the statement said.

Italy, a founder member of the European Economic Community 40 years ago, is determined not to be left behind in EMU and Prime Minister Romano Prodi has already drawn up a bitter 1997 budget to cut 62.5 trillion lire ($37 trillion) off the deficit.
Less than two months after pushing that unpopular package through parliament, Prodi's announcement of a new mini-budget is intended to prove Italy is no slouch about its EMU commitments.

The government is unlikely to unveil the size of the mini-budget until state accounts are released next month, but analysts are forecasting it will contain deficit cuts of 10-20 million lire. Several expect a 13-15 trillion lire range.
"Italy can bring nothing but stability to the European Union," Ciampi told Reuters Financial Television.

"There's no doubt that we have another problem -- reducing the public sector borrowing requirement. The Italian government is committed to doing this," he said, adding the mini-budget will "ensure that this commitment is fully respected".

Ciampi told reporters after his talks and lunch with Zalm that he was optimistic that Eurostat, the EU body which oversees government accounting practices, would approve a controversial 5.5 trillion lire "Euro-tax" contained in Italy's 1997 budget.

Eurostat is due to issue its ruling on Friday and if it rejects the measure, Italy's hopes of making EMU in the first wave would probably be ruined. However, analysts expect Eurostat to give Italy the green light.

But Italy still faces an uphill battle on EMU. German public opinion, already reluctant to give up the mighty mark, fears the presence of Italy with its erratic public finances record could result in a weakening of the single European currency, the euro.
Questions have arisen that the whole project may be delayed as even Germany, where unemployment is rising worryingly, struggle to meet the Maastricht criteria.
Zalm said he was not concerned. Asked whether he thought EMU would be delayed, he said: "No, I don't think so."
He praised Italy's decision to pass a mini-budget. "I think it is important that it proves the strength of the Italian government towards reaching a decent budget," he told reporters.
Economists say the mini-budget is vital to achieving a key Maastricht goal, that of trimming the ratio between Italy's deficit and gross domestic product (GDP) to 3.0 percent.

EU states will be judged on their EMU fitness in early 1998. The closely-watched deficit-GDP ratio ballooned to 6.8 percent last year after the deficit overshot forecasts and hit 138.5 trillion lire. But analysts said a mini-budget could cut it to just above 3.0 percent.
